name: The rational decision model
origin: Classical economics (Smith, Ricardo, Walras); Jones & George (2008)
purpose: How would a perfectly rational decision maker decide?

parts.label: Problem
points: Recognise the problem and the need to decide

parts.label: Diagnose
points: Synoptic evaluation from one point of view

parts.label: Alternatives
points: List ALL alternatives, analyse each independently
All consequences in time and space, compare

parts.label: Choose
points: Best course of action – optimise the firm's value system

apply: Use it as the benchmark: which step was skipped or impossible in the case?
pitfalls: A utopia: ignores time constraints and limits of knowledge and information processing
example: Decision fatigue: Obama wore only grey or blue suits to save decisions.

name: Bounded rationality vs rational model
purpose: How do real decision makers decide?

parts.label: Bounded rationality – satisfice
points: Incomplete, imperfect information; limited cognition and time
FIRST satisfactory solution, respects the status quo

apply: Show how limited information, time and cognition led to a “good enough” choice
pitfalls: Satisficing ≠ irrational: it is rational within limits
example: Chirac's 1997 dissolution of the National Assembly; Kahneman: “we're blind to our blindness”.

name: Organisations as decision-support systems
purpose: How do organisations help overcome bounded rationality?

parts.label: Hierarchy & control
points: No need to question orders; releases responsibility

apply: Link each mechanism to the course: Taylor/Mintzberg, Weber/Milgram, bureaucracy, Crozier
pitfalls: The same mechanisms can also hinder: rigidity, agentic state, filtered information

name: Carnegie model
purpose: How does an organisation – not an individual – decide?

parts.label: Negotiated goals
points: Production, inventory, market share, sales, profits

parts.label: Sub-problems
points: Each sub-group uses its standard procedures

parts.label: Satisfice
points: Stop at the first solution acceptable to the hierarchy

apply: Ask: which coalitions exist, whose goals won, which local solutions were stuck together?
pitfalls: Not one rational decision maker – conflicts between sub-groups are normal

name: Group decision-making
purpose: Are two heads better than one?

parts.label: Weaknesses
points: Domination by a few; social loafing (Ringelmann)
Denial of intuition; sobriety of expression

apply: Boards, executive committees, juries: weigh commitment against conformity
pitfalls: Polarisation = more extreme decision, not a compromise
example: Sobriety of expression: pilots and control tower minimise warning signals.

name: Groupthink – 8 symptoms
purpose: Why do cohesive groups make faulty decisions?

parts.label: Mindguards
points: Shield group and leader from contradictory information

apply: Find symptoms in the case, then the risk factors: similar backgrounds, insulation, no decision rules
pitfalls: Cohesion alone is not groupthink – look for the symptoms
example: Pearl Harbor, Bay of Pigs, Vietnam, Iran hostage rescue, Iraq invasion.

name: Allison's three models
purpose: Through which lenses can one decision be explained?

parts.label: Bounded rationality
points: Individuals with limited resources, time, cognition

parts.label: Organisational model
points: Shaped by organisational processes and features

parts.label: Political model
points: Output of negotiation between actors with own interests

apply: Analyse the same decision three times; link lens 2 to Sessions 3–5 and lens 3 to Session 6
pitfalls: The lenses complement each other – use all three, not one
example: Cuban Missile Crisis 1962: US response to Soviet missiles in Cuba.
